title: Seqlen-aware E2E trace field notes
content:
Context:
These are field notes from a short investigation into how end-to-end request latency and per-stage timing change as a function of sequence length (seqlen) and cache/coldstart state. Goal: produce a compact, actionable picture we can use for routing/autoscale heuristics and a set of follow-ups to reduce p95/p99 regressions observed in the last two weeks.

Quick summary of findings:
- Latency scales non-linearly with sequence length; model-forward time dominates and becomes the large majority of p95/p99 at seqlen >= 512.
- Small seqlen (<= 64): network and pre/post-processing variance contributes a non-trivial share of p95; batching and KV cache lookups can reduce p50 but adds tail risk if lock contention occurs.
- Cold-start traces show a distinct early-stage spike (container init + model jit/warmup) that mostly affects p99; warm requests show steady per-token cost.
- Observed a recurring 60–120ms jitter in routing+auth stage on ~3% of traces correlated with our internal rate limiter token bucket refill timing.

Experimental setup (how traces were collected):
- Time window: 2026-02-16 -> 2026-02-18; synthetic replay using our trace-playback tool against a dedicated pool (4x A100 80GB nodes), model: open-llama-13b-quant (quantized serving variant), batch sizes: 1 (single-token streams) and 4, request mix: generation-only (no tool calls).
- Trace instrumentation: per-request tag propagation, stage boundaries: client-recv -> ingress-proxy -> auth/router -> tokenization -> routing-to-pool -> kv-cache-lookup -> batch-aggregation -> model-forward -> kv-cache-update -> postprocess -> client-send.
- Aggregation: grouped by measured generated sequence length buckets: [<=32], [33-128], [129-512], [513-2048]. For each bucket we computed p50/p95/p99 and per-stage median fraction of total latency.

Numeric snapshot (median fractions and latency buckets) — representative numbers from warm runs (batch=1):
- seqlen <= 32: p50=32ms, p95=68ms, p99=120ms. Per-stage median fraction: ingress+auth 5%, tokenization 8%, routing+queue 4%, kv-lookups 3%, model-forward 75%, postprocess 5%.
- seqlen 33-128: p50=54ms, p95=180ms, p99=430ms. Per-stage: ingress+auth 4%, tokenization 6%, routing+queue 3%, kv 4%, model-forward 80%, postprocess 3%.
- seqlen 129-512: p50=125ms, p95=420ms, p99=1.2s. Per-stage: ingress+auth 3%, tokenization 4%, routing+queue 3%, kv 6%, model-forward 82%, postprocess 2%.
- seqlen 513-2048: p50=430ms, p95=1.8s, p99=4.2s. Per-stage: ingress+auth 2%, tokenization 3%, routing+queue 2%, kv 7%, model-forward 85%, postprocess 1%.

Cold-start vs warm behavior:
- Cold starts (container spin + model load) add a delta of ~800ms to p50 and up to ~2.5s to p99 depending on node warmup. The cold spike is almost entirely in the routing-to-pool and model-forward first-iteration steps (disk load/JIT).
- Subsequent warm requests settle to the numbers above; however if the node has been idle >10 minutes we see a smaller but measurable tail due to page reclaim and GPU context reinitialization.

Detailed observations and hypotheses:
1) Model-forward dominates tail growth with seqlen: p99 grows faster than p95 as sequence length increases because occasional scheduling preemption or CUDA kernel fallback causes multi-100ms stalls. Hypothesis: kernel selection path sometimes falls back to slower kernels for certain attention patterns.
2) KV-cache lookup contributes more in mid-range seqlens: when long prefixes are present we hit more cache activity and lock contention on the async cache update path. Hypothesis: per-request serialization in the cache writer thread is producing spikes at scale.
3) Ingress/auth jitter correlated with rate limiter refill: traces with auth-stage spikes line up with token-bucket refill events on our ingress proxies. Hypothesis: the proxy performs a synchronous DB check on rare rate-limit boundary cases (old code path).
4) Batch aggregation sometimes increases p95 for small seqlen: with batch-size=4 we saw p50 improve but p95 regress for seqlen<=32 because a single slow request holds up other requests in the batch if we wait the full batching window. Hypothesis: current batch timer logic doesn't early-release when N==batch-size and picks up slow stragglers.

Action items (short-term):
- (A1) Add an experiment to pin kernel selection to the fast path for common attention sizes and compare p99 (owner: Marco, JIRA-ENG-4831).
- (A2) Add per-request KV cache writer timing and change writer to lock-free append (owner: Liang, spike branch linked).
- (A3) Patch ingress proxy to avoid synchronous DB lookups on token bucket boundary; replace with local approximate counters + async reconciliation (owner: Riley).
- (A4) Adjust batch timer heuristic: if batch_count > 1 and leading-candidate latency > threshold then flush early (owner: Aisha).
- (A5) Add long-idle node warmup probe (small synthetic request) triggered at 5m idle to avoid page reclaim tail (owner: SRE lead).

Longer-term research points:
- Investigate dynamic kernel replanning: measure whether compiling a small set of specialized kernels per-seqlen reduces p99 without harming p50.
- Explore KV cache sharding by prefix-hash to reduce writer contention on long-prefix workloads (esp for conversational apps).
- Study batching vs latency SLOs: build an SLO-aware batching controller that trades throughput vs tail depending on active latency budget per-route.

Open questions / things to validate:
- Does the fallback kernel happen only on certain GPU driver versions? Need matrix of driver+cuda+cudnn versions from traces.
- How common are long-prefix cache update bursts from real customer traffic vs synthetic replay? We should correlate with production RT logs.
- What is the cost/benefit of a 5m warmup probe (extra small requests) vs keeping nodes pinned (cost implications)?

Useful trace excerpts and examples (ids):
- trace-id: 20260217-ff12a (seqlen=480, p99 spike from kernel fallback; see GitHub PR for instrumentation).
- trace-id: 20260216-88b0c (cold start; large model disk load observed).

Notes to self / first-pass checklist for next run:
- Run the same replay against a different quantized model and on T4 pool to compare kernel fallback behavior.
- Toggle batch timer to experiment with early-release flush + get per-route impact.
- Export full set of driver/cuda versions for all nodes that produced p99 traces.

If you read this and have thoughts, drop inline comments or ping me in #eng-serving-runtime. This is intentionally a field-notes style doc; goal is to capture the oddball tails we saw and a short list of experiments to reduce them.
